descs.t: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race, and former Congressman Hansen Clarke followed her. Michigan voters on camera say her move changed their vote. We walk through what she said and how her party answered.

Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, now says he is unfit to serve in the Senate and is campaigning for Mike Rogers. CNN reports that multiple House Democrats are privately pushing to expel her from their caucus. We look at what her break means for the Michigan race.

Haley Stevens said she does not like seeing the Democratic nominee campaign with somebody who said America deserved 9/11, and she backed Mike Rogers. Her party turned on her, and some Michigan Democrats are following her anyway. This is the fight inside the Democratic Party on Election Day.

intro.plain: Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for Senate in Michigan, over her own party's nominee, Abdul El-Sayed. Then former Congressman Hansen Clarke did the same. Voters on camera say it gave them permission to switch. It is Election Day, so this matters right now. Chat, tell me: is crossing party lines an act of conscience, or a betrayal?
intro.mid: Haley Stevens lost the Michigan Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed by about one percent. Now she calls him unfit for the Senate and is campaigning for Mike Rogers. CNN reports some House Democrats want her out of their caucus. On Election Day, the question is whether Democrats follow her. Chat, if you are in Michigan, did her move change anything for you?
intro.bold: A sitting Democrat looked at her party's Senate nominee, saw him standing with somebody who said America deserved 9/11, and said no. Haley Stevens backed Mike Rogers, and her own party went after her for it. Some Michigan voters say she gave them permission to switch. Chat, would you have had the guts to do what she did?

hook.plain: A Democratic congresswoman just endorsed the Republican in Michigan's Senate race. Here is what Haley Stevens said, who followed her, and how her party answered.
hook.mid: Haley Stevens lost the primary by about one percent. Now she is campaigning for the other side. Here is why, and what it could mean for Michigan's Senate race.
hook.bold: She was called a traitor for saying no to Abdul El-Sayed. Haley Stevens did not back down, and some Michigan Democrats are following her. Here is the whole fight.

descs.t: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots that federal officials flagged as possible noncitizen votes, AP reports. A late night Ninth Circuit ruling and a block from Judge James Boasberg came first. We walk through how the case got here.

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stop California counting roughly 20,000 mail ballots it says came from likely noncitizens, and the Court said no. We look at what the three rulings said, what California officials warned, and what it means for the midterm count.

About 20,000 California mail ballots flagged by the federal government as possible noncitizen votes will not be set aside, after the Supreme Court turned down the Trump administration. One side calls it protecting voters, the other calls it a hole in election integrity. Here is the fight, and the question it leaves open.

intro.plain: The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration's request to make California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots. Federal officials flagged them as possible noncitizen votes. Before that, the Ninth Circuit and Judge James Boasberg had also ruled against the request. So California keeps counting. Chat, should flagged ballots be counted while the checks are still going on?
intro.mid: The Trump administration went to the Supreme Court in a last ditch effort to stop California counting roughly 20,000 mail ballots it says came from likely noncitizens. The Court said no. That is three courts in a row. Chat, tell me: is this courts protecting voters, or courts ignoring a real problem?
intro.bold: Twenty thousand California mail ballots, flagged by the federal government as possible noncitizen votes, and the Supreme Court just refused to set them aside. California calls the federal push interference. The administration calls it protecting the vote. Chat, if you were on the Court, how would you have ruled?

hook.plain: The Supreme Court just turned down the Trump administration on 20,000 California ballots. Here is what was asked, what the courts said, and what happens to the count.
hook.mid: Three courts, one answer: California keeps counting. Here is why the Trump administration lost its fight over 20,000 flagged mail ballots.
hook.bold: Twenty thousand ballots flagged as possible noncitizen votes, and the Supreme Court will not stop them being counted. Here is the fight over who gets checked, and who decides.

descs.t: A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit over the state's Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan appears on the ballot beside Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. We walk through what the suit asked for, why it was thrown out, and what happens next.

Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the DOJ's Decoy Dan lawsuit in Alaska, and the department says it is appealing. President Trump says Chuck Schumer and Marc Elias should be held responsible for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while one poll shows Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. We look at how a duplicate name could matter under ranked choice.

Two men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's Senate ballot, a court just tossed the DOJ's attempt to step in, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. With the race tied in one poll, every confused ballot could count. We break down the fight, the appeal, and whether voters can trust the result.

intro.plain: A federal judge in Alaska has thrown out the Justice Department's lawsuit over the Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan is on the ballot next to the real Senator Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. So what was the suit about, and does it change anything before the vote? Chat, have you ever seen two candidates with the same name on one ballot?
intro.mid: Alaska's Senate race has two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, and a judge just dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit over it. The DOJ is appealing, Trump is blaming Schumer and Marc Elias, and one poll has Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. In a race that close, a name could matter. Chat, tell me: is this a dirty trick or a nothing story?
intro.bold: Two Dan Sullivans, one Senate seat, and a race tied at 50 percent in one poll. A judge just tossed the DOJ's lawsuit, the DOJ says it will appeal, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. If a duplicate name decides Alaska, who answers for it? Chat, call it: should a decoy name ever be allowed on a ballot?

hook.plain: A judge has dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit over Alaska's Senate ballot, which carries two Dan Sullivans. The DOJ says it will appeal. Here is what the case was about.
hook.mid: Alaska's Senate race is tied in one poll, and there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. A judge just threw out the DOJ's challenge. Here is what that means.
hook.bold: Two Dan Sullivans on one ballot, a dead even race, and a lawsuit just tossed out of court. Here is how a single name could decide Alaska's Senate seat.

descs.t: The United States carried out what officials call defensive strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters and AP report. Axios reports the strikes came after the Islamic Republic's forces fired a missile toward American aircraft, and that the launcher was destroyed. We walk through what is known so far.

US forces struck Qeshm Island the night before the midterm elections, after a missile was reportedly fired at American aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, the regime told Reuters that a deal to end the war remains far off. We look at what the strikes change for the talks and for Hormuz.

The Islamic Republic's forces fired at American aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz, and within hours a US strike destroyed the launcher on Qeshm Island, according to Axios. Trump says the regime built an anti aircraft facility there, and the US took some out. This is what deterrence looks like.

intro.plain: The United States has carried out what officials call defensive strikes on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz. Axios reports the regime's forces fired a missile toward American aircraft first, and the launcher was destroyed. This came the night before the midterms. Chat, do you see this as self defense, or the start of a new round?
intro.mid: US forces hit Qeshm Island last night after a missile was reportedly fired at American aircraft over Hormuz. And the regime is telling Reuters a deal to end the war is still far off. So strikes are up, talks are stuck. Chat, what do you think the Islamic Republic does next?
intro.bold: The Islamic Republic fired a missile at American aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz. Within hours, a US strike took out the launcher on Qeshm Island, according to Axios. Trump says they built an anti aircraft facility there and the US took some out. Chat, does the regime have anything left to answer with?

hook.plain: A missile fired toward American aircraft, and then US strikes on Qeshm Island. Here is what officials say happened in the Strait of Hormuz.
hook.mid: Strikes on Qeshm Island, and the regime saying a deal is far off, all on the eve of the midterms. Here is what it means for the war.
hook.bold: The regime fired at American jets over Hormuz. Hours later its launcher on Qeshm Island was gone. Here is how it happened, and what it tells us.
